title: iJoy – Participatory Development and Evaluation of the Efficacy of an Inclusive Internet-Based Treatment for Genito-Pelvic Pain/Penetration Disorder
summary:
This study further develops and scientifically evaluates an existing online treatment for women experiencing pain and difficulties during sex. Participants experience a sexual dysfunction known as Genito-Pelvic Pain/Penetration Disorder (GPPPD) and face difficulties, pain, tension, or fear during vaginal penetration, despite having a desire for sexual activity.
The online treatment will be improved to better meet the diverse needs of participants – regardless of relationship status, sexual orientation, or current sexual activity. To achieve this, online focus groups will gather feedback from individuals who have previously been affected: What helped them? What would they like to see improved? Based on this input, the treatment will be adapted and then tested in a scientific study to determine whether the online treatment can help reduce sexual distress and alleviate symptoms.
conditions: The diagnosis of Genito-Pelvic Pain/Penetration Disorder (GPPPD) was introduced in the Fifth Edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) and combines the previously separate categories of dyspareunia (sexual pain disorder) and vaginismus (sexual penetration disorder). This change was made due to the high overlap of symptoms and the lack of evidence for clear differential diagnostic distinctions (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). GPPPD is defined by four main features: (1) difficulties with vaginal penetration, (2) vulvovaginal or pelvic pain, (3) fear or anxiety about vaginal pain, and (4) tensing or tightening of the pelvic floor muscles during attempted vaginal penetration (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). For a diagnosis, at least one of these core symptoms must have been present for a minimum of six months and must cause clinically significant distress.  This new diagnostic category has also been included in the Eleventh Revision of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD-11) under the term “genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder.” It is classified as a distinct disorder within the group of diseases of the genitourinary system. While vaginismus is covered under this category, dyspareunia is not classified as a sexual dysfunction but rather as a non-inflammatory disorder of the female genital tract (World Health Organization, 2019).

interventions.name: Participants in the intervention group will receive access to a self-help-based, guided, inclusive internet-based intervention (IMI) called “iJoy” for the treatment of Genito-Pelvic Pain Penetration Disorder (GPPPD). The IMI consists of eight weekly core sessions, a booster session four weeks later,

Participants in the Waitlist Control Group will gain access to the IMI six months after randomization. Until then, they will not receive any therapeutic support for their sexual difficulties and will serve as a control group to account for time-dependent effects.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Focus Groups and Think-Aloud Testing:
Participants are eligible if they:
- self-report that they meet the DSM-5 criteria for a diagnosis of Genito-Pelvic Pain Penetration Disorder (GPPPD) in the past,
- speak and understand German fluently,
- voluntarily provide written informed consent, and
- have access to an internet-enabled device.

RCT:
For the evaluation study, participants must:
- have been assigned female at birth and currently have female anatomy
- be able to read and understand German sufficiently well,
- voluntarily provide written informed consent,
- have access to an internet-enabled device, and
- meet the diagnostic criteria for GPPPD according to DSM-5, confirmed by trained study staff using the DISEX-F (Schwesig et al., 2024). 
Participants will be also asked in a self-report whether they have already undergone a medical evaluation to rule out medically treatable causes for their symptoms. If not, they will be encouraged to do so before continuing with the study. In addition, scores ≥ 11 on the FSDS-R must indicate clinically relevant sexual distress (Derogatis et al., 2002).
Exclusion criteria:
RCT:
Additional exclusion criteria assessed via self-report include:
- current or past psychotic disorder,
- current post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD),
- current alcohol or substance dependence,
- current moderate to severe depression,
- current mania,
- or current pregnancy or within the first 8 weeks postpartum.
- Women cannot participate if they are already receiving psychotherapy or any other treatment for GPPPD at study start, or if they are on a waiting list for another treatment during the study period. 
The diagnosis is made if at least one core criterion has been present for at least six months and the symptoms cannot be better explained by another nonsexual mental disorder, significant relationship distress (e.g., partner violence), or major stressors. The disorder should also not be solely attributable to the effects of a substance, medication, or a medical condition. Certain physical illnesses (e.g., current cancer treatment) that could make participation overly burdensome for the woman are also considered exclusion criteria.
